title: Walk through the bug life cycle (New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Verified → Closed) and the alternate states (Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, Deferred, Not Reproducible) — and how do you handle a bug a developer says they "cannot reproduce" (capture exact environment/version/data/steps, logs, video/screenshots, network trace, and a minimal deterministic repro)?
shortTitle: The bug life cycle, alternate states, and handling a "cannot reproduce" defect

s1_definition.profdef: The bug life cycle is the sequence of states a defect moves through from discovery to closure: New when first logged, Assigned when given to a developer, Open while being worked, Fixed when the code change is done, Retest when the tester re-verifies, Verified when the fix is confirmed, and Closed when the defect is fully resolved. Alternate states handle non-linear outcomes: Reopened when a supposedly fixed bug recurs, Rejected when it is not a valid defect, Duplicate when it matches an existing bug, Deferred when a valid bug is postponed, and Not Reproducible when the developer cannot recreate it. A cannot-reproduce bug is handled by supplying the exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, video, and network trace, ideally reduced to a minimal deterministic reproduction.
s1_definition.analogy: When a teller at the National Bank of India spots a problem, say the balance screen shows a wrong figure, it starts as a New complaint. It is handed to an engineer, Assigned, who starts work, Open, makes the repair, Fixed, hands it back for the teller to re-check, Retest, the teller confirms it is correct, Verified, and the ticket is filed away, Closed. Sometimes the path bends: the problem comes back, Reopened; the engineer says it is working as designed, Rejected; someone already reported it, Duplicate; it is real but will wait until next release, Deferred; or the engineer simply cannot make it happen on their machine, Not Reproducible. For that last case, the teller must hand over the exact branch, the app version, the specific account and amounts, the precise click-by-click steps, screen recordings, and the system logs, so the engineer can finally see it happen.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The bug life cycle is the sequence of states a defect moves through from discovery to closure: New when first logged, Assigned when given to a developer, Open while being worked, Fixed when the code change is done, Retest when the tester re-verifies, Verified when the fix is confirmed, and Closed when the defect is fully resolved. Alternate states handle non-linear outcomes: Reopened when a supposedly fixed bug recurs, Rejected when it is not a valid defect, Duplicate when it matches an existing bug, Deferred when a valid bug is postponed, and Not Reproducible when the developer cannot recreate it. A cannot-reproduce bug is handled by supplying the exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, video, and network trace, ideally reduced to a minimal deterministic reproduction.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a teller at the National Bank of India spots a problem, say the balance screen shows a wrong figure, it starts as a New complaint. It is handed to an engineer, Assigned, who starts work, Open, makes the repair, Fixed, hands it back for the teller to re-check, Retest, the teller confirms it is correct, Verified, and the ticket is filed away, Closed. Sometimes the path bends: the problem comes back, Reopened; the engineer says it is working as designed, Rejected; someone already reported it, Duplicate; it is real but will wait until next release, Deferred; or the engineer simply cannot make it happen on their machine, Not Reproducible. For that last case, the teller must hand over the exact branch, the app version, the specific account and amounts, the precise click-by-click steps, screen recordings, and the system logs, so the engineer can finally see it happen.

**One line to remember:** A bug flows New to Assigned to Open to Fixed to Retest to Verified to Closed, with alternate states Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, Deferred, and Not Reproducible, and you defeat a "cannot reproduce" by handing over exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, video, and a minimal deterministic repro.

sections.s2_technical:
The standard flow begins at New when the tester logs a defect with a clear title, steps, expected and actual results, and evidence. A triage or lead then moves it to Assigned by giving it to a developer. When the developer begins investigating, it becomes Open, sometimes called In Progress. Once the developer commits a fix, it becomes Fixed, and the build carrying that fix is deployed to a test environment. The tester then re-runs the scenario, which is the Retest state, and if the bug is gone and nothing else broke, the tester marks it Verified. Finally the defect is Closed, meaning it is fully resolved and needs no further action.

The alternate states handle real-world non-linearity. Reopened happens when a Fixed-and-closed bug recurs, often because the fix was incomplete or a regression reintroduced it; the tester reopens rather than filing a brand new bug so history is preserved. Rejected, sometimes called Not a Bug or Working as Designed, is used when the reported behavior is actually correct per the requirements or is a misunderstanding; good practice is for the developer to explain why so the tester can learn or escalate. Duplicate marks a defect that is the same underlying issue as an existing one, and you link the two so the fix on the original resolves both. Deferred marks a valid bug that the business consciously postpones, typically because it is low priority and the release cannot wait; it stays in the backlog with a reason. Not Reproducible is used when the developer cannot recreate the failure, which is where the interesting work lies.

Handling a cannot-reproduce bug well is a senior skill because non-reproducibility is usually a symptom of missing context, not a non-existent bug. The disciplined response is to gather and attach everything that could differ between the tester's and developer's worlds. That means the exact environment, operating system, browser and version, device, and which deployed environment; the exact build or version of the application and its dependencies; the exact data, the specific account identifiers, amounts, and any special state such as an account that is dormant or over a limit; the exact reproduction steps in precise order, with no assumed knowledge; and rich evidence, a screen recording or screenshots at the moment of failure, the application and server logs correlated by a request or trace identifier, and a browser network trace or HAR file showing the actual request and response. The goal is to reduce the problem to a minimal deterministic reproduction, the smallest set of steps and data that reliably triggers the failure, because determinism is what converts a hand-waving "sometimes it breaks" into a bug a developer can fix. Common hidden causes that non-reproducibility exposes are environment differences, time zone or locale, specific data states, race conditions and timing, cached state, feature flags, or an authentication and permission difference. The senior nuance is to treat Not Reproducible as a collaboration prompt rather than a dead end: you add the missing context, and if it still cannot be reproduced you instrument the code with extra logging and wait for it to recur in production with correlation identifiers, so that the next occurrence is captured with everything needed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A tester at the National Bank of India finds that a transfer shows a wrong balance, and the defect must move through clear states so everyone knows who owns it and what stage it is at. This is exactly the bug life cycle: New, Assigned, Open, Fixed, Retest, Verified, Closed.

Problem 2 — A developer marks a different bug Not Reproducible because it works on their machine. The tester must supply exact environment, version, data, steps, logs, and a trace to make it deterministic. This is exactly the cannot-reproduce workflow.

Problem 3 — Some reports are not real defects or already exist, so the model must support Reopened, Rejected, Duplicate, and Deferred as valid outcomes.

In the mini-project we build a defect state machine that enforces legal transitions, records a reproduction bundle, and demonstrates resolving a Not Reproducible bug by attaching the missing context so it becomes reproducible and progresses to Fixed. We define a `BugState` enum, a `ReproBundle` capturing environment, version, data, steps, and evidence, a `Defect` holding its current state and bundle, and a `BugWorkflow` that validates transitions and logs the journey.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two defects, one a clean wrong-balance bug, one an intermittent dormant-account failure that the developer cannot reproduce.

Step 1: The happy-path defect moves New to Assigned to Open as the developer picks it up and investigates. Each transition is validated against the allowed-transitions map.

Step 2: The developer fixes it, so it moves Open to Fixed, the build deploys, and the tester re-runs it in Retest, confirms it, and marks it Verified, then Closed. The full linear journey is logged.

Step 3: The second defect moves New to Assigned to Open, but the developer cannot recreate it, so it moves Open to Not Reproducible.

Step 4: The tester tries to push it back to Open without supplying context. The workflow guard blocks the transition because the reproduction bundle is incomplete, enforcing the discipline that non-reproducibility needs more information.

Step 5: The tester attaches the complete bundle, exact environment, exact version, exact data including the dormant-over-one-hundred-eighty-days state, precise steps, and evidence including a video, a correlated server log trace identifier, and a network HAR file. Now the guard passes, the bug returns to Open, and the developer, finally able to see it deterministically, fixes it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The bug life cycle is the set of states a defect moves through from discovery to closure. It starts at New when I log it with clear steps, expected and actual results, and evidence; moves to Assigned when a developer owns it; to Open while they investigate; to Fixed when the code change lands; to Retest when I re-run the scenario against the new build; to Verified when I confirm the fix and that nothing else broke; and finally to Closed. Around that main line are the alternate states that reflect reality: Reopened when a closed bug recurs, which preserves history instead of filing a new one; Rejected when the behavior is actually correct or a misunderstanding; Duplicate when it matches an existing defect and the two are linked; Deferred when a valid bug is consciously postponed with a reason; and Not Reproducible when the developer cannot recreate it.

Handling a cannot-reproduce bug is where I show seniority, because non-reproducibility almost always means missing context rather than a non-existent bug. My response is to supply everything that could differ between my world and the developer's: the exact environment including operating system, browser, version, and which deployed environment; the exact application build; the exact data including specific account identifiers, amounts, and special states such as a dormant account; the precise ordered steps with nothing assumed; and rich evidence, a screen recording, the server and application logs correlated by a request or trace identifier, and a browser network or HAR trace. My goal is a minimal deterministic reproduction, the smallest steps and data that reliably trigger it, because determinism is what lets a developer actually fix it. If it still will not reproduce, I instrument the code with extra logging keyed by a correlation identifier and wait for the next occurrence so it is captured completely.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this discipline. We once had an intermittent debit failure that a developer marked Not Reproducible; I reproduced it only after noticing it happened only on accounts dormant for more than one hundred eighty days, so I attached that data state, the exact staging build, click-by-click steps, a screen recording, and a server log with the matching trace identifier, and the developer fixed it within the day. I also treat Not Reproducible as a collaboration prompt, not a dead end, and I always capture a workaround and the affected population in the report. Being able to walk the full life cycle including the alternate states, and to explain concretely how I turn a cannot-reproduce into a deterministic repro, is what tells an interviewer I manage defects like an experienced engineer rather than just filing tickets.
